The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra and some of the Kufians recited it as to drown its people with the ta’ in to drown, and the people are in the accusative case, meaning: to drown you, O man, the people of this ship with the hole that was torn in it. The majority of the reciters of Kufa recited it as to drown its people with the ya’ in the nominative case, on the basis that the people are the ones who drown. The correct thing to say about this, in my opinion, is: They are two well-known readings that are widespread in the readings of the regions, and they agree in meaning even if their wording differs. So whichever one the reader reads, he is correct. We said: They are in agreement in meaning, because it is known that Moses’ denial of the world’s breach of the ship was only because he believed that this would be a cause for the drowning of its people if such an event happened in it. The meaning of this is not hidden from anyone. It was read with the ta’ and the accusative of the people, or with the ya’ and the nominative of the people.

evidence.text: The reciters differed in the recitation of His statement, to drown its people.

The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra and some of the Kufians recited it as to drown its people with the ta’ in to drown, and the people are in the accusative case, meaning: to drown you, O man, the people of this ship with the hole that was torn in it.
The majority of the reciters of Kufa recited it as to drown its people with the ya’ in the nominative case, on the basis that the people are the ones who drown.
The correct thing to say about this, in my opinion, is: They are two well-known readings that are widespread in the readings of the regions, and they agree in meaning even if their wording differs.
It was read with the ta’ and the accusative of the people, or with the ya’ and the nominative of the people.

x: The Almighty says: He said to Moses when he said to him what he said, Did I not tell you that you would never be able to have patience with me over what you see of my actions, because you see what you do not know about.
Moses said to him,
h
Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot
The people of interpretation differed about the meaning of that.

Some of them said: This speech from Moses, peace be upon him, to the scholar was a contradiction, not that he had forgotten his covenant, and what had preceded it when he accompanied him with his saying, But if you follow me, do not ask me about anything until I mention it to you.
Those who said that mentioned:

c: It was narrated on the authority of Yahya bin Ziyad,
m: who said: Yahya bin Al-Muhallab narrated on the authority of a man, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Abi bin Kaab Al-Ansari, regarding his statement,
h
Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot
. He said: He did not forget, but it is one of the metaphors of speech.

x: Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: Do not hold me accountable for abandoning your covenant. The reason is that the meaning of forgetfulness is abandonment.
Those who said this were mentioned:

c: Ibn Hamid told us, he said: Salamah told us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq told us, on the authority of al-Hasan ibn Ammarah, on the authority of al-Hakam, on the authority of Saeed ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: He said, ‘
h
Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot

,’ meaning for what I left out of your covenant. The correct thing to say about this is that Moses asked his companion not to hold him accountable for what he forgot about his covenant with him asking him about the way he did and the reason for it, not for what he asked him about while he was remembering the authentic hadith from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, that this is part of the meaning of the report, and that is what:

c: Abu Kuraib narrated to us, he said: Yahya bin Adam narrated to us, he said: Ibn Uyaynah narrated to us, on the authority of Amr bin Dinar, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of Ubayy bin Ka’b, on the authority of the Messenger of God,
m: h
Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot

. He said: The first was from Moses forgetfulness. And His statement, And do not burden me with hardship in my affair, means: Do not deceive me with hardship in my affair, meaning: Do not make my affair with You and my companionship with You difficult for me.

x: God the Almighty says: So they set out, until they met a boy, and he killed him. The scholar, then Moses said to him: Have you killed
h
a pure soul
? The reciters differed in the recitation of that, so most of the reciters of Hijaz and Basra recited it as I have killed
h
a pure soul
and they said that its meaning is: the purified one who has no sin, and has never sinned because of her youth. Most of the reciters of Kufa recited it as
h
a pure soul
meaning: the repentant one whose sins have been forgiven.
Mention of those who said that:

c: Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: Did you kill
h
a pure soul
? The pure soul is the one who repents.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: “He said: Did you kill
h
a pure soul
?” He said: The pure soul is the repentant one.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us,
m: Did you kill
h
a pure soul
? He said: Al-Hasan said: Repentant, thus in the hadith of Al-Hasan and it is famous: pure.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn,
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubayd narrated to us, who said: I heard Ad-Dahhak say regarding His statement,
h
A pure soul
, that he said: Repentant. He mentioned those who said: Its meaning is the Muslim one who has no sin.

c: Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj,
m: saying: Yaʿla ibn Muslim informed me that he heard Saʿid ibn Jubayr say: Al-Khidr found some boys playing, so he took a charming boy, laid him down, and then slaughtered him with a knife. He said: Wahb ibn Sulayman informed me, on the authority of Shuʿayb al-Jubbaʿi, saying: The name of the boy whom Al-Khidr killed was Jaysur. He said: Did you kill
h
a pure soul
? He said: Muslim. He said: Ibn Abbas read it as Zakiya like you say: Zakatana.

x: Some of the scholars of the Arabic language from Kufa used to say: The meaning of Zakiya and Zakiya is one, like Qasiyya and Qasiyya. He used to say: It is the one that has not committed any sin. And that is what is correct in my opinion, because I have not found any difference between them in any of the Arabic speech. If that is the case, then whichever of the two readings that reciter recited is correct, because they are two readings that are widespread in the readings of the regions with the same meaning. His saying, without a soul, means: without retaliation for a soul that was killed, so killing was required in retaliation for it. His saying,
h
You have certainly done something reprehensible
, means:
h
You have certainly done something reprehensible
, and you have committed an unacceptable act. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said.
Who said that?

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: h
You have certainly done something reprehensible
. Reprehensible is more severe than imr.

evidence.text: The reciters differed in the recitation of that, so most of the reciters of Hijaz and Basra recited it as I have killed a pure soul and they said that its meaning is: the purified one who has no sin, and has never sinned because of her youth.
Most of the reciters of Kufa recited it as a pure soul meaning: the repentant one whose sins have been forgiven.
He said: Ibn Abbas read it as Zakiya like you say: Zakatana.
If that is the case, then whichever of the two readings that reciter recited is correct, because they are two readings that are widespread in the readings of the regions with the same meaning.

x: God Almighty says: The scholar said to Moses, Did I not tell you that you would never be able to have patience with me regarding what you see of my actions that you do not know about?

Moses said to him: If I ask you about anything after this meaning: after this time do not accompany me meaning: then leave me, do not be my companion I have reached an excuse from me meaning: I have reached an excuse in my case. The reciters differed in the recitation of that, so most of the reciters of Medina recited it from me an excuse with a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal, and a lightened noon. Most of the reciters of Kufa and Basra recited it with a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal, and a shaddah on the noon.

Some of the reciters of Kufa recited it with a damma on the lam, a sukoon on the dal, and a lightened noon. It is as if those who stressed the noon sought to keep the noon in la-dun from moving, since it was originally silent, and if it had not been stressed it would have moved, so they stressed it out of their dislike of moving it, as they did with min and 'an when they added them to the two places of the one reporting about himself, so they stressed them, and said minni and 'ani. As for those who lightened it, they found that the one who is reporting on himself in the case of the lowering is a ya’ alone, without a nun with it. So they did that from the beginning according to what their speech did in that with all other things besides it. The correct thing to say about this, in my opinion, is that they are two eloquent languages, and each of them has been recited by scholars of the Qur’an, so whichever of them the reciter recites is correct.

However, the reading that I like the most in this regard is the reading with the fatha on the lam, the damma on the dal, and the shaddah on the nun, for two reasons: One of them is that it is the more famous of the two languages, and the other is that Muhammad ibn Nafi’ al-Basri told us, he said:

c: Umayyah ibn Khalid told us, he said: Abu al-Jariyah al-Abdi told us, on the authority of Abu Ishaq, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka’b,
m: that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, recited I have conveyed an excuse from Me with emphasis.

c: Abdullah bin Abi Ziyad told me: Hajjaj bin Muhammad told us, on the authority of Hamza al-Zayyat, on the authority of Abu Ishaq, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of Abi bin Kaab, on the authority of the Prophet,
m: may God bless him and grant him peace, similarly. He mentioned that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, recited this verse and said: Moses was ashamed for God’s sake.

c: Muhammad bin Al-Muthanna told us: Badal bin Al-Muhabbir told us: Ibad bin Rashid told us: Dawud told us,
m: regarding the words of God Almighty: “If I ask you about anything after this, do not accompany me. You have received an excuse from Me.” He said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Moses felt shy for God’s sake at that time.

c: Abdullah bin Abi Ziyad told me: Hajjaj bin Muhammad told us, on the authority of Hamza al-Zayyat, on the authority of Abu Ishaq, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of Abi bin Kaab, who said:
m: Whenever the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, mentioned someone and prayed for him, he would start with himself. One day he said: May God have mercy on us and on Moses. If he had stayed with his companion, he would have seen the wonder. But he said: If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep company with me. You have received a burdensome excuse from me.

evidence.text: The reciters differed in the recitation of that, so most of the reciters of Medina recited it from me an excuse with a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal, and a lightened noon.
Most of the reciters of Kufa and Basra recited it with a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal, and a shaddah on the noon.
Some of the reciters of Kufa recited it with a damma on the lam, a sukoon on the dal, and a lightened noon.

The correct thing to say about this, in my opinion, is that they are two eloquent languages, and each of them has been recited by scholars of the Qur’an, so whichever of them the reciter recites is correct.

However, the reading that I like the most in this regard is the reading with the fatha on the lam, the damma on the dal, and the shaddah on the nun, for two reasons: One of them is that it is the more famous of the two languages, and the other is that Muhammad ibn Nafi’ al-Basri told us, he said:
He mentioned that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, recited this verse and said: Moses was ashamed for God’s sake.

x: God Almighty says: So Moses and the scholar set out, “until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food, but they did not feed them. They offered them hospitality, but they refused to host them. Then they found therein a wall about to collapse.” He says: They found in the town a wall about to collapse and fall. It is said from this: the house collapsed, if it collapsed and fell, and from this comes the collapse of the star. This is its fall and removal from its place, and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah: Then he swooped down like a shining star It was narrated on the authority of Yahya bin Ya’mar that he read that, intending to destroy it.
The scholars of Arabic speech differed in their meaning when it was read in this way.

Some of the people of Basra among them said: It is a metaphor for yanqad meaning it is uprooted from its root and cracks, similar to their saying: Qad anqadat as-san meaning it has cracked and has cracked from its root. It is said: Firaq ka qayd as-san meaning its people will not meet.

Some of the people of Kufa among them said: Anqiyad is a crack in the length of the wall in the folds of a well or in a man’s tooth. It is said: Qad anqadat as-san meaning it has split lengthwise. It was said: The village whose people asked Moses and his companion for food, but they refused to host them, was Al-Ayla.
Who said that?

c: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dhar’i’ told me:
m: ‘Umar ibn al-Mu’tamir, the companion of al-Karabisi, told us: Hammad Abu Salih told us, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: They went to al-Aylah, for few come to it and return disappointed. It is the land to which they refused to host them, and it is the land farthest from the sky from God.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: his statement, So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town, and he recited to his statement, I would have taken payment for it, the worst of towns is the one that does not host guests, and does not recognize the right of the wayfarer.

x: The scholars of the Arabic language differed regarding the meaning of God Almighty’s statement, He wants to destroy it.

Some of the people of Basra said: The wall has no will, nor does the dead, but if it is in this case from the ruins, then it is his will. This is like what the Arabs say about something else: The spear wants Abu Baraa's chest and he wants the blood of Bani Aqil Another of them said: He only spoke to the people with what they understand. He said: That is because it was close to collapsing. It is permissible for him to say: He wants to collapse. He said: And similar to it is: The heavens almost burst and their saying: I almost fly with joy, and you did not come close to that, and you did not care about it, but the matter is very serious to you. And some of the Kufians among them said: It is from the speech of the Arabs to say: The wall is about to fall. He said: And similar to it from the speech of the Arabs is the saying of the poet: A time that surrounds me with a camel for a time that intends to do good And the other said: My camel complains to me about the length of the journey.

Be patient, for we are both afflicted. He said: The camel did not doubt, but he spoke about it on the basis that if he had spoken, he would have said that. He said: And so is the saying of Antarah: I visit the one who was struck by the spear and complained to me with tears and snorted He said: And from this is the saying of God the Almighty: And when Moses’ anger subsided, and anger does not subside, but rather its companion subside, and its meaning is: it subsides. And His saying: And when the matter is decided, it is only the people who decide it. Another of them said: This is from the most eloquent speech of the Arabs. And he said: The meaning of the wall is its inclination, as the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: Their two fires are visible, and it is that there are two fires, each one from the other in a place where if a person stood in it he would see the other in proximity.

He said: And it is like the saying of God the Almighty about the idols: And you will see them looking at you, but they do not see. He said: And the Arabs say: My house looks at the house of so-and-so, meaning the proximity between them, and he cited as evidence the saying of Dhu al-Rummah in his description of a pond or a dilapidated house: He almost did or was about to do it He said: So he made it important, but its meaning is that it has changed due to wear and tear. What we say about that is that God, the Almighty, in His kindness, made speech between His creation out of mercy towards them, so that some of them might explain to others what is in their hearts, which their eyes cannot perceive. The Arabs understood the meaning of the saying: On a mission, her heads were worried about her, as axes worry about cutting, and she understood that axes are not described by what the sons of Adam are described by, from the consciences of the chests, while describing her as wanting, and she knew what the speaker meant when he said: Like a hill, the pedestrians are covered with dust at times and the dust at other times.

Rather, He did not mean that the dust spoke, but rather that it was covered with dew, which prevented it from pouring down. So preventing it from doing so was like preventing someone with logic from pouring down. Likewise, His statement, a wall about to collapse, you know that its meaning is: it is about to fall or collapse. Rather, the Most High addressed with the Qur’an the one through whose tongue the revelation was sent down, and they understood what He meant, even though the dull and blind were unable to understand it, and the ignorant and foolish were led astray by it. His saying, So he erected it. It was mentioned on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: He demolished it and then sat down to build it.

c: Ibn Hamid told us that: Salamah told us that: Ibn Ishaq told us, on the authority of Al-Hasan Ibn Ammarah, on the authority of Al-Hakam Ibn Utaybah, on the authority of Saeed Ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas.
m: And others said about that what:

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Amr ibn Dinar, on the authority of Saeed ibn Jubayr,
m: And they found therein a wall about to collapse. He said: He lifted the wall with his hand and it stood straight. The correct thing to say about this is that God, the Exalted, informed us that the companion of Moses and Moses found a wall that was about to collapse, so the companion of Moses straightened it, meaning: he adjusted its tilt until it became level. It is possible that this was due to repair after it had been demolished. It is possible that this was due to him raising it with his hand, so it became level by the power of God, and its tilt was removed by His kindness. There is no evidence from the Book of God or any report of the excuse that is decisive as to which of these things it was from. And His statement, He said, ‘If you wished, you could have taken payment for it,’ means that Moses said to his companion, If you wished, you could not have straightened the wall of these people until they gave you payment for your erection.

x: Some of them said, What Moses meant by the payment that he said to him, ‘If you wished, you could have taken payment for it,’ was hospitality, meaning until they hosted us, for they refused to host us.

Others said: Rather, he meant by that the compensation and reward for building the leaning wall. The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Kufa read it as If you wished, you would have taken a reward for it, based on their interpretation of it as if it were from the verb to take.

Some of the people of Basra read it as If you wished, you would have taken with a light ta’ and a kasra on the kha’. Its original form is lafa’alt, except that they made the ta’ as if it were part of the root of the word. This is because the speech, according to them, is in the form of fa’ala and yayfa’ul from that: takhadhu fulan kadha yatakhadahu takhadan, which is a language, as mentioned by Hudhayl. Some poets said: My feet have been planted beside me, like the hammers of a sandpiper. The correct thing to say about this, in my opinion, is that they are two well-known dialects of the Arabs with one meaning. Whichever one the reader reads, he is correct. However, I choose to read it with a shaddah on the ta’ of la-ta’ala, because it is the more eloquent and famous of the two dialects, and the one most often used by the Arabs.

However, I choose to read it with a shaddah on the ta’ of la-ta’ala, because it is the more eloquent and famous of the two dialects, and the one most often used by the Arabs.

x: God Almighty says: The companion of Moses said to Moses: What you said, which is His statement, If you had willed, you could have taken payment for it, “is a separation between me and you,” meaning: a separation between me and you: meaning a separation between me and you. Shall I inform you? He says: I will tell you the interpretation of that which you could not have patience for? He says: what the consequences of my actions that I knew would lead to, so you could not have patience to stop asking about them and to stop criticizing me for them. And God knows best.
He says: As for what I did to the ship, it was because it belonged to poor people who worked at sea, so I wanted to damage it with the holes I made in it.

c: As Ibn Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: regarding the statement of God Almighty, So I wanted to fault it, he said: I would tear it apart.

c: Al-Harith told us, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: the same.

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: the same. And his saying,
h
And behind them was a king who seized every ship by force
, and in front of them and ahead of them was a king.

c: As Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said: Abd Al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: And behind them was a king. Qatada said: In front of them. Do you not see that he says, Behind them is Hell, and it is in front of them?

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, he said:
m: It was in the recitation: And before them was a king who seized every intact ship by force. And it was mentioned on the authority of Ibn Uyaynah, on the authority of Amr, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he recited that: And before them was a king.

x: Some of the people who know the Arabic language have made raa one of the letters of opposites, and he claimed that it refers to what is in front of it and what is behind it, and he cited as evidence for the validity of that the words of the poet: I hope that the Banu Marwan will listen to me and obey me, and my people Tamim and the desert behind them Meaning in front of me, and he has overlooked the correct aspect of that. Rather, what is in front of him is said: He is behind me, because you are behind him. So you will meet him as he will meet you, so it became: when he was meeting you, it was as if he was behind you and you were in front of him.

Some of the Arab scholars from Kufa did not allow it to be said to a man in front of you: he is behind me, nor if he was behind you to be said: he is in front of me, and he said: this is only permissible in times of days and times like the saying of the one who says: behind you is severe cold, and in front of you is severe heat, because you are behind it, so it was permissible because it is something that comes, so it is as if if it catches up with you it becomes behind you, and as if if you reach it it becomes in front of you. He said: therefore the two meanings are permissible. And his saying:
h
He seizes every ship by force the speaker says

: what benefit did this scholar's tearing of the ship he boarded from its people, since because of its tearing he seizes all the ships, defective and non-defective, and what was the reason for his justification for tearing it, that he tearing it, because behind them is a king who seizes every ship by force?
It was said: The meaning of this is that he would take every sound ship by force, and leave every defective one, not that he would take the sound ones and the unsound ones.
What is the evidence that this is the case?
His saying,
h
So I wanted to find fault with it

, thus made clear that he only found fault with it because the defective ones were not exposed to it, so it was sufficient for it to be said: And behind them was a king who would take every sound ship by force, although this is also the case in some readings.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, on the authority of Mal:
m: It is in the wording of Ibn Masoud: And behind them was a king who seized every good ship by force.

c: Ibn Hamid told us: Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, who said: Al-Hasan bin Dinar told us, on the authority of Al-Hakam bin Uyaynah, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said:
m: In my father’s reading: And behind them was a king who seized every good ship by force, and I only blamed it to turn him away from it.

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Husayn told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj,
m: And behind them was a king who would seize every ship by force. So when they succeeded him, they would repair it with pitch and enjoy it. Ibn Jurayj said: Wahb ibn Sulayman told me, on the authority of Shu’ayb al-Jubba’i, that the name of the man who would seize every ship by force was Hadad ibn Badad.

And it was mentioned on the authority of Ibn Uyaynah, on the authority of Amr, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he recited that: And before them was a king.

He says, he would overwhelm them with transgression, which is arrogance towards God and disbelief in Him. And similar to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said, and it was mentioned in some letters: As for the boy, he was a disbeliever.
Mention of those who said that:

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: As for the boy, he was a disbeliever in the letter of Abi: And his parents were believers. So we intended that their Lord should substitute for them one better than him in purity and nearer to kinship.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: And as for the boy, his parents were believers. And he was a disbeliever in some readings. His saying: So we feared. And it is in the Mushaf of Abdullah: So your Lord feared that He would overburden them with transgression and disbelief.

c: Amr ibn Ali told us: Abu Qutaybah told us: Abdul-Jabbar ibn Abbas al-Hamadani told us, on the authority of Abu Ishaq, on the authority of Saeed ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka’b,
m: that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: The boy whom al-Khidr killed was marked as an unbeliever on the day he was marked. The Arabs direct fear and dread to the meaning of suspicion, and these letters are directed to the meaning of knowledge of something that is perceived through something other than the senses and sight. We have explained that with its evidence in other places, so there is no need to repeat it.

x: Some of the Arab scholars from Basra used to say: The meaning of his saying we feared in this place is: we hated, because God is not feared. And he said in some of the readers: So fear your Lord. He said: It is like the two men feared that they would be dependent, and he does not fear that more than he hates it for them.

evidence.text: And he said in some of the readers: So fear your Lord.

h
So We intended that their Lord should substitute them
: The reciters differed in the recitation of that, so a group of the reciters of Mecca, Medina, and Basra recited it,
h
So We intended that their Lord should substitute them

Some of them used to justify the validity of that by saying that it was found stressed in most of the Qur'an, like the statement of God, the Almighty, So those who wronged substituted, and His statement,
h
And when We substituted a verse for another verse

: so the correct statement is, So We intended that He should substitute them with it. The majority of the reciters of Kufa recited that, So We intended that He should substitute them with a light dal.

i: Some of those who recited that in the same way from the people of Arabic said:
x: Abdal yabdal with a light dal and badal yabdal with a heavy dal have the same meaning.
The correct thing to say about this in my opinion is that they are two readings with similar meanings.

A group of reciters have recited each of them, so whichever one the reciter recites, he is correct. It has been said that God Almighty replaced the parents of the boy whom Moses’ companion killed with a girl.
Those who said this: Yaqub told me, he said:

c: Hashim bin Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Mubarak bin Saeed told us, he said: Amr bin Qais told us
m: regarding His statement,
h

. He said: It has reached me that she is a girl.

m: he heard Yaqub ibn Asim say: They replaced the boy with a girl. Ibn Jurayj said: Abdullah ibn Uthman ibn Khathim told me that he heard Saeed ibn Jubayr say: They replaced the boy with a girl.

Mention of those who said that:

m: h
So we intended that their Lord should substitute for them one better than him in purity and nearer to kinship
. He said: His mother was pregnant at that time with a Muslim boy.

m: that he mentioned the boy whom Al-Khidr killed, and he said: His parents were happy with him when he was born and grieved for him when he was killed, and if he had lived, it would have led to their destruction. So let a person be satisfied with the decree of God, for God’s decree for the believer in what he dislikes is better for him than His decree in what he likes. And his saying,
h
Better than him in zakat
, means: Better than the boy he killed in terms of righteousness and religion.

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj,
m: his statement,
h
So we intended that their Lord should substitute for them one better than him in purity
, he said: Islam. And his saying, and closer in kinship, the people of interpretation differed in its interpretation.

x: Some of them said: The meaning of that is: and closer in mercy to his parents and more dutiful to them than the one who was killed.
Those who said that mentioned:

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Muammar told us on the authority of Qatada:
m: And the closest of kin means the most pious to him.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:

x: Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: It is more likely that his parents will have mercy on him than the one who was killed.

x: Some of the Arab scholars interpreted that as: And closer to have mercy on him. Womb is the source of mercy. It is said: I had mercy on him with mercy and compassion.

Some of the Basrans used to say: From womb and kinship. And it may be said: womb and womb like ‘asr and ‘asr, and halaka and halaka. And he cited as evidence for his statement the verse of Al-Ajjaj: And the womb of those who are crooked is not crooked There is no point in the womb in this context, because the murdered person was the one whose parents God replaced with a son for the murdered person’s parents, so their kinship to his parents and their kinship to him in the womb are the same. Rather, the meaning of that is: And it is closer to the murdered person that he shows mercy to his parents and is dutiful to them, as Qatada said. The statement may be directed to its meaning being: And it is closer to them showing mercy to him, but no one among the people of interpretation Surat al-Kahf 18:81 So We intended that their Lord should substitute for them one better than him in purity and nearer to kinship. interpreted it in this way, so since there is no one who interpreted it, then what we said is correct in it, for what we have explained.

m: And there was a treasure under it for them. He said: Knowledge.

c: Muhammad bin Al-Muthanna told us, he said: Abu Dawud told us, he said: Shu’bah told us, on the authority of Abu Hasin, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair,
m: And there was a treasure under it for them. He said: Knowledge.

c: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us,
m: all on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, his statement,
h
And there was beneath it a treasure for them
, he said: scrolls for two boys in which there was knowledge.

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, he said:
m: The pages of knowledge.

c: Ahmad bin Hazim Al-Ghafari told me: Hanada bint Malik Al-Shaibaniyyah told us:
m: I heard my friend Hammad bin Al-Walid Al-Thaqafi say: I heard Jaafar bin Muhammad say about the statement of God Almighty:
h
And beneath it was a treasure for them both

. He said: Two lines and a half, the third was not completed: I am amazed at the one who is certain of provision how he tires himself, and I am amazed at the one who is certain of the reckoning how he is heedless, and I am amazed at the one who is certain of death how he rejoices when He said: And if there be the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth, and sufficient are We as reckoners. She said: It was mentioned that they were preserved by the righteousness of their father, and no righteousness was mentioned from them, and between them and the father by whom they were preserved were seven fathers, who was a weaver.

c: Yaqub told me, he said: Al-Hasan bin Habeemb bin Nadbah told us, he said: Salamah bin Muhammad told us, on the authority of Na’im al-Anbari,
m: who was one of Al-Hasan’s companions, he said: I heard Al-Hasan say, regarding His statement,
h
And beneath it was a treasure for them both

, he said: A golden tablet on which was written: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful: I am amazed at the one who believes, how he can grieve, and I am amazed at the one who is certain of death, how he can rejoice, and I am amazed at the one who knows the world and its vicissitudes with its people, how he can be reassured by it. There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the Messenger of God.

c: Ibn Hamid told us, he said: Salamah told us, he said: Ibn Ishaq told me, on the authority of Al-Hasan bin Ammarah, on the authority of Al-Hakam, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: that he used to say: The treasure was nothing but knowledge.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Ibn Uyaynah told us, on the authority of Hamid, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: regarding his statement,
h
And there was beneath it a treasure for them
, he said, Pages of knowledge.

c: Yunus told me, he said: Ibn told us, he said: Abdullah bin Ayyash told me, on the authority of Omar,
m: the freed slave of Ghafra, he said: The treasure that God said in the Surah in which the cave is mentioned, And beneath it was a treasure for them, he said: It was a solid gold tablet, on which was written: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. I am amazed at someone who knew death and then laughed. I am amazed at someone who was certain of destiny and then became weary. I am amazed at someone who was certain of death and then felt secure. I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger.

x: Others said: Rather, it was hidden wealth.
Those who said that mentioned:

c: Yaqub told me, he said: Hisham told us, he said: Hisin told us, on the authority of Ikrimah:
m: And there was a treasure beneath it for them. He said: A treasure.

c: Ibn Bashar told us, he said: Abd al-Rahman told us, he said: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Abu Hasin, on the authority of Ikrimah,
m: the same.

c: Ibn Al-Muthanna told us: Abu Dawud told us, on the authority of Shu’bah, who said: Abu Husayn told me, on the authority of Ikrimah,
m: something similar. Shu’bah said: We did not hear it from him.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: And beneath it was a treasure for them. He said: It was money for them. Qatada said: The treasure was made permissible for those who came before us, and forbidden for us. For God makes permissible whatever He wills of His command, and forbids, and they are the Sunnahs and the obligatory duties. He makes permissible for one nation and forbids for another, but God does not accept from anyone who has passed away except sincerity and monotheism for Him. The first of the two interpretations is the correct one: the statement made by Ikrimah, because it is known from the speech of the Arabs that the treasure is the name for whatever is hoarded of money, and that everything that is hoarded has the name treasure applied to it. So the interpretation is diverted to the most common usage of those addressed by the revelation, unless there is evidence that requires diverting it to something else, for reasons that we have explained in more than one place. And His statement,
h
And their father was Salih

, and your Lord intended that they should reach maturity, means: So your Lord intended that they should reach maturity and strength and then extract their treasure hidden under the wall that you had erected, out of mercy from your Lord for them. He says: You did this to the wall, out of mercy from your Lord for the orphans. And Ibn Abbas used to say about that what:

c: Musa bin Abdul Rahman told me: Abu Usamah told us, on the authority of Misa’ar, on the authority of Abdul Malik bin Maysarah, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubayr, who said:
m: Ibn Abbas said, in his statement,
h
And their father was righteous
, he said: They were preserved by the righteousness of their father, and what was mentioned of their righteousness.

c: Abu Kuraib told us: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Misa’ar, on the authority of Abd al-Malik ibn Maysarah, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: similarly. And his statement,
h
And I did not do it of my own accord
, means: And I did not do, O Moses, all that you saw me do of my own accord, and of my own accord. Rather, I did it based on God’s command to me.

c: As Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: h
And I did not do it of my own accord
. He was a servant who was commanded, so he carried out God’s command.

c: Ibn Humayd told us: Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq:
m: And what I did of my own accord means I have not seen anything that I did of my own accord. And His statement: That is the interpretation of that over which you were not able to have patience means: What is the interpretation of what I mentioned to you of the reasons for which I did the actions that you found reprehensible from me? He says: What is the interpretation of the actions that you were not able to leave off asking Me about and your denouncing them with patience? These stories that God Almighty told His Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, about Moses and his companion, are a lesson from Him to him, and a warning to him to stop hastening the punishment of the polytheists who denied Him and mocked Him and His Book, and an announcement from Him to him that His actions towards them, even if they happened as the eyes see, in a way that might sometimes happen to His friends, their interpretation leads them to the conditions of His enemies in them, just as the actions of Moses’ companion were contrary to what appeared to be correct in Moses’s eyes, since he was not aware of their consequences, while they were correct in reality and would eventually lead to the truth. The correctness of that is indicated by His statement: “
h
And your Lord is the Forgiving

, the Merciful. If He were to impose blame on them for what they have earned, He would have hastened the punishment for them. Rather, for them is an appointed time from which they will not find any refuge.” Then he followed that with the story of Moses and his companion, teaching his prophet that his leaving the punishment of these polytheists to be hastened, without looking at them, even if that is what one who has no knowledge of what God has planned for them thinks, is looking at them, because the interpretation of that leads to their destruction and ruin by the sword in this world and their deserving of eternal disgrace from God in the Hereafter.

x: God the Almighty says to His Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him: And these polytheists ask you, O Muhammad, about Dhul-Qarnayn, what was his affair and what was his story. So say to them: I will recite to you a mention of his story. He says: I will relate to you a story about him. It has been said that those who asked the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, about the affair of Dhul-Qarnayn were people from the People of the Book. As for the report that those who asked him about that were polytheists from his people, we have mentioned it before.
As for the report that those who asked him were people of the Book:

c: Abu Kuraib narrated it to us.
m: He said: Zaid bin Habbab narrated to us on the authority of Ibn Lahi’ah. He said: Abd al-Rahman bin Ziyad bin An’am narrated to us on the authority of two sheikhs from Tajib. One of them said to his companion: Let us go to Uqbah bin Amir so that we may talk. They said: So they went to him and said: We have come so that you may talk to us. He said: One day I was serving the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and I left him and some people from the People of the Book met me. They said: We want to ask the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. He asked permission for us to see him, so I entered upon him and told him. He said: What do I have to do with them? I have no knowledge except what God has taught me. Then he said: Pour me some water. So he performed ablution and prayed. He said: Before he finished, I could see the joy on his face. Then he said: Bring them in to me, and whoever you see of my companions. So they entered and stood before him. He said: If you wish, you may ask, and I will tell you what you find written in your book, and if you wish, I will tell you. They said: Yes, tell us. He said: You came to ask me about Dhul-Qarnayn, and what you find written in your book. He was a young man from the Romans. He came and built the city of Alexandria in Egypt. When he finished, an angel came to him and lifted him up to the sky. He said to him: What do you see? He said: I see my city and cities. Then he ascended with him. He said: What do you see? He said: I see my city. Then he ascended with him and said: What do you see? He said: I see the earth. He said: This sea surrounds the world. Indeed, God has sent me to you to teach the ignorant and to confirm the knowledgeable. So he brought him the dam, which is two soft mountains that everything slips from. Then he went with him until he passed Gog and Magog. Then he went with him to another nation, their faces are the faces of dogs fighting Gog and Magog. Then he went with him until he cut off another nation fighting those whose faces are the faces of dogs. Then he went with him until he cut off these to another nation that he named.

x: The scholars differed about the meaning for which Dhul-Qarnayn was called Dhul-Qarnayn.
Some of them said: He was called that because he was struck on his horn and perished, then he was revived and struck on the other horn and perished.
Those who said that mentioned:

c: Ibn Hamid told us: Hakam told us, on the authority of Anbasa, on the authority of Ubayd al-Maktab, on the authority of Abu al-Tayyil, who said:
m: Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali about Dhul-Qarnayn, and he said: He is a servant who loved God and He loved him, and he advised God and He advised him, so he commanded them to fear God, so they struck him on his horn and killed him, then God resurrected him, so they struck him on his horn and he died.

c: Muhammad bin Bashar told us: Yahya told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Habib bin Abi Thabit, on the authority of Abu al-Tayyib, who said:
m: Ali, may God be pleased with him, was asked about Dhul-Qarnayn, and he said: He was a servant who advised God and God advised him. He called his people to God, and they struck him on his horn and he died, but God revived him. He called his people to God, and they struck him on his horn and he died, so he was called Dhul-Qarnayn.

c: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told us: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar told us: Shuʿbah told us, on the authority of al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza, on the authority of Abu al-Tayyal, who said:
m: I heard Ali, and they asked him about Dhul-Qarnayn: Was he a prophet? He said: He was a righteous servant who loved God and God loved him, and he advised God and God advised him. Then God sent him to his people, and they struck him twice on the head, so he was called Dhul-Qarnayn, and there is someone like him among you today.

x: Others said about that as follows:

c: Muhammad bin Sahl al-Bukhari narrated to me, saying: Ismail bin Abdul Karim narrated to us, saying: Abdul Samad bin Maqal narrated to us, saying: Wahb bin Munabbih said:
m: Dhul-Qarnayn was a king. It was said to him: Why was he called Dhul-Qarnayn? He said: The People of the Book differed concerning him.

x: Some of them said: The king of the Romans and Persians.
Some of them said: He had something like two horns on his head.
Others said: He was called that because the two sides of his head were made of copper.
Those who said that are mentioned:

c: Ibn Hamid told us: Salamah told us: Ibn Ishaq told us: Someone I do not accuse told me on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih al-Yamani:
m: He was called Dhul-Qarnayn because the two sides of his head were made of copper.

x: And His statement, Indeed, We established him upon the earth and gave him from every thing a means, means: We established him upon the earth. And We gave him from every thing a means, means: We gave him from every thing: meaning what leads to it, which is knowledge of it. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said.
Who said that?

c: Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: his statement,
h
And We gave him a reason for everything
, meaning: knowledge.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: his statement,
h
And We gave him a reason for everything
: meaning knowledge.

c: Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said:
m: Ibn Zayd said, in his statement,
h
And We gave him a reason for everything
, he said: Knowledge of everything.

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj,
m: his statement,
h
And We gave him a reason for everything
, he said: knowledge of everything.

c: Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: h
And We gave him a reason for everything
knowledge.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Hussein,
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubaid narrated to us, who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say regarding His statement, And We gave him a cause for everything, meaning: knowledge.

x: And his saying, So he followed a path. The readers differed in their reading of that. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra read it as so he followed with the alif connected and the ta' doubled, meaning: he walked and traveled, from the saying of the speaker: I followed the trace of so-and-so: if I followed him and walked behind him. The majority of Kufa readers read it as Fataba’a with a hamza on the alif and a light ta’, meaning caught up. The first of the two readings in this regard is the correct reading: the reading of the one who read it as fa-taba’a with the alif connected and the ta’ doubled, because this is report from God Almighty about the journey of Dhul-Qarnayn in the land in which he was empowered, not about his reaching the cause, and this is how the interpretation of the people of interpretation came.
Who said that?

c: Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: Then he followed a cause, meaning by cause: the home.

c: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us,
m: both on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding his statement a cause, he said: a home and a path between the east and the west.

c: Al-Qasim told me, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: something similar.

c: Muhammad bin Amara Al-Asadi told me: Ubaid God bin Musa told us: Israel told us, on the authority of Abu Yahya, on the authority of Mujahid:
m: Then he followed a path, he said: A path on the earth.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: h
Then he followed a way
: he followed the dwellings of the earth and its landmarks.

c: Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said
m: regarding His statement,
h
Then follow a way
, he said: This is now the way of the paths, as Pharaoh said, O Haman, build me a tower that I may reach the ways, the ways of the heavens, he said: The ways of the heavens.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement,
h
Then he followed a way
, he said: The dwellings of the earth.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn,
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubayd told us, who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say, in his statement,
h
Then follow a way
, he said: The stations.

evidence.text: The readers differed in their reading of that.

The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra read it as so he followed with the alif connected and the ta' doubled, meaning: he walked and traveled, from the saying of the speaker: I followed the trace of so-and-so: if I followed him and walked behind him.
The majority of Kufa readers read it as Fataba’a with a hamza on the alif and a light ta’, meaning caught up.

The first of the two readings in this regard is the correct reading: the reading of the one who read it as fa-taba’a with the alif connected and the ta’ doubled, because this is report from God Almighty about the journey of Dhul-Qarnayn in the land in which he was empowered, not about his reaching the cause, and this is how the interpretation of the people of interpretation came.

x: God Almighty says: Until when he reached the setting of the sun, he found it setting in a hot spring. The reciters differed in their recitation of this.
Some of the reciters of Medina and Basra recited it in a hot spring, meaning that it sets in a hot spring of water.
A group of the reciters of Medina and most of the reciters of Kufa recited it in a hot spring, meaning that it sets in a hot spring of water.
The interpreters differed in their interpretation of this, just as the reciters differed in their reading of it. He mentioned the one who said, He set in a hot spring.

c: Muhammad bin Al-Muthanna told us: Ibn Abi Uday told us, on the authority of Dawud, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: He found it setting in a murky spring. He said: In black mud.

c: Ibn Al-Muthanna told us, he said: Abd Al-A’la told us, he said: Dawud told us, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: that he used to recite in a hot spring. He said: one with hot mud.

c: Al-Husayn ibn al-Junayd narrated to us, saying: Saʿid ibn Muslimah narrated to us, saying: Ismail ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, on the authority of Uthman ibn Hadir,
m: saying: I heard Abdullah ibn Abbas say: Muʿawiyah recited this verse and said: A hot spring. Ibn Abbas said: It is a hot spring. He said: So they put Kaʿb between them. He said: So they sent to Kaʿb al-Ahbar and asked him, and Kaʿb said: As for the sun, it sets in Thaʿt, so it was as Ibn Abbas said, and Thaʿt is mud.

c: Yunus told us, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Nafi’ ibn Abi Na’im told me, he said:
m: I heard Abd al-Rahman al-A’raj say: Ibn Abbas used to say, in a murky spring, then he explained it as: having murky mud. Nafi’ said: Ka’b was asked about it, and he said: You are more knowledgeable about the Qur’an than I am, but I find it in the Book that it disappears into black mud.

c: Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: He found it setting in a murky spring. He said: It is the murky water.

c: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid:
m: In a hot spring. He said: Tha’t.

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: regarding the statement of God Almighty, set in a spring of murky water, he said: Tha’ata. He said: Amr bin Dinar informed me, on the authority of Ata bin Abi Rabah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: I read in a hot spring, and Amr bin Al-Aas read in a hot spring. So we sent to Ka’b, and he said: It sets in a hot, black mud.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: It sets in a hot spring. Hot spring means black mud.

c: Muhammad bin Abdul A’la told us: Marwan bin Mu’awiyah told us, on the authority of Warqa’, who said:
m: I heard Saeed bin Jubair say: Ibn Abbas used to recite this letter in a hot spring and say: Black mud in which the sun sets.

x: Others said: Rather, it disappears in a hot spring.
Who said that?

c: Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: He found it setting in a hot spring. He said: in a hot spring.

c: Yaqub told us, he said: Ibn Ulayyah told us, on the authority of Abu Raja’, he said:
m: I heard Al-Hasan say, In a hot spring. He said: Hot.

c: Al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Muammar informed us, on the authority of al-Hasan,
m: regarding his statement, in a hot spring, he said: Hot, and al-Hasan read it in this way. The correct thing to say about that, in my opinion, is that they are two readings that are widespread in the readings of the regions, and each one of them has a correct aspect and an understood meaning, and neither of its aspects corrupts the other, and that is because it is possible for the sun to set in a hot spring with hot mud, so the reader would be describing it with the characteristic that it has, which is hot, and the reader would be describing it with the characteristic that it has, which is mud and mud. And it was narrated with both of its forms, which I said are from its characteristics, report.

c: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told us: Yazid ibn Harun told us: Al-Awam told us: A client of Abdullah ibn Amr told me, on the authority of Abdullah, who said:
m: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, looked at the sun when it set and said: In the blazing fire of God, in the blazing fire of God. Were it not for the command of God that restrains it, it would have burned everything on the earth.” Surat al-Kahf 18:86 Until, when he reached the setting of the sun, he found it setting in a spring of murky water. And he found near it a people. We said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them or you take good care of them."

c: Al-Fadl bin Dawud Al-Wasiti told me: Abu Dawud told us: Muhammad bin Dinar told us, on the authority of Saad bin Aws, on the authority of Musaddaa, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of Abi bin Kaab,
m: that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, recited to him Ham’ah. And His statement,
h
And he found there a people

, He mentioned that those people were called asik. And His statement, We said, ‘O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them,’ He said, “either you kill them if they do not enter into the acknowledgment of the Oneness of God and submit to what you call them to in terms of obeying their Lord. “Or you take good care of them,” He said, or you take them captive and teach them guidance and show them the right path.

The interpreters differed in their interpretation of this, just as the reciters differed in their reading of it.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Junayd narrated to us, saying: Saʿid ibn Muslimah narrated to us, saying: Ismail ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, on the authority of Uthman ibn Hadir, saying: I heard Abdullah ibn Abbas say: Muʿawiyah recited this verse and said: A hot spring.

Muhammad bin Abdul A’la told us: Marwan bin Mu’awiyah told us, on the authority of Warqa’, who said: I heard Saeed bin Jubair say: Ibn Abbas used to recite this letter in a hot spring and say: Black mud in which the sun sets.

Al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Muammar informed us, on the authority of al-Hasan, regarding his statement, in a hot spring, he said: Hot, and al-Hasan read it in this way.

The correct thing to say about that, in my opinion, is that they are two readings that are widespread in the readings of the regions, and each one of them has a correct aspect and an understood meaning, and neither of its aspects corrupts the other, and that is because it is possible for the sun to set in a hot spring with hot mud, so the reader would be describing it with the characteristic that it has, which is hot, and the reader would be describing it with the characteristic that it has, which is mud and mud.

x: He, the Most High, says: “He said: As for he who does wrong, We will punish him.” He continues: As for he who disbelieves, We will kill him.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement, But as for him who has wronged, We will punish him, he said: It means killing. And his statement,
h
Then he will be returned to his Lord

, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment, he said: Then he will return to God Almighty after being killed, and He will punish him with a great punishment, which is the terrible punishment, and that is the punishment of Hell.

x: He says: As for he among them who believed in God and believed in Him alone, and acted in obedience to Him, then for him is the best with God, which is Paradise, as a reward, meaning a recompense for his faith and obedience to his Lord. The reciters differed in the recitation of this, so most of the reciters of the people of Medina and some of the people of Basra and Kufa recited it, For him is the best reward, raising the recompense and adding it to the best. If this is recited in this way, then there are two interpretations: One of them is that the best is meant to refer to his faith and righteous deeds, so the meaning of the statement, if this is what is meant by it, is: As for he who believes and does righteous deeds, then for him is its reward, meaning the reward for these good deeds. The second interpretation is that what is meant by the best is Paradise, and the reward is added to it, as it was said, And the home of the Hereafter is better, and the home is the Hereafter, and as it was said, And that is the religion of right, and the religion is the right.

Others read: For him is the best reward, meaning: For him is Paradise as a reward. So the reward is in the accusative case as a source, meaning: He will reward them with the reward of Paradise. The more correct of the two readings in this, in my opinion, is the reading of the one who read it: For him is the best reward, with the accusative case of the reward and its tanween, according to the meaning that I described, that they will have Paradise as a reward. So the reward is in the accusative case as an explanation. And His statement: And We will speak to him from Our command with ease, means: And We will teach him in this world what is easy for us to teach him, which will bring him closer to God and soften our speech to him. And Mujahid used to say something similar to what we said about that.

m: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us.

c: And Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us,
m: all of them, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, his statement, Of Our command, ease, he said, well-known.

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: the same.

evidence.text: The reciters differed in the recitation of this, so most of the reciters of the people of Medina and some of the people of Basra and Kufa recited it, For him is the best reward, raising the recompense and adding it to the best.

If this is recited in this way, then there are two interpretations: One of them is that the best is meant to refer to his faith and righteous deeds, so the meaning of the statement, if this is what is meant by it, is: As for he who believes and does righteous deeds, then for him is its reward, meaning the reward for these good deeds.

The more correct of the two readings in this, in my opinion, is the reading of the one who read it: For him is the best reward, with the accusative case of the reward and its tanween, according to the meaning that I described, that they will have Paradise as a reward.

x: God Almighty says: Then Dhul-Qarnayn proceeded and took paths and stations.

c: As Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: regarding his statement,
h
Then he followed a path
, meaning a home.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: Then he followed a way the houses of the earth and its landmarks.

x: Until, when he reached the place of sunrise, he found it rising on a people for whom We had not made any shield against it. God Almighty says: And Dhul-Qarnayn found the sun rising on a people for whom We had not made any shield against it. This was because their land had no mountains or trees, and could not support buildings, so they lived in houses, but rather sank into the water or crept into the streams.

c: Ibrahim bin Al-Mustamir told me, he said: Sulayman bin Dawud and Abu Dawud told us, they said: Sahl bin Abi Al-Salt Al-Siraj told us, on the authority of Al-Hasan:
m: It will rise upon a people for whom We have not made any shelter from it. He said: It was a land that could not support building, and when the sun rose upon them they would sink into the water, and when it set they would come out to graze their flocks, as animals graze. He said: Then Al-Hasan said: This is the hadith of Samurah.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: Until, when he reached the place of sunrise, he found it rising on a people for whom We had not made any shelter against it. He mentioned to us that they were in a place where no building could stand, but rather they would be in groups of theirs, until when the sun had passed their zenith, they would go out to their livelihoods and their fields. He said: Thus, We have encompassed what he had in knowledge.

c: Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj,
m: regarding his statement,
h
And he found it rising upon a people for whom We had not made any shelter besides it

, he said: They had never built a building in it, and no building was ever built upon them in it. And when the sun rose upon them, they would enter flocks that had the right to the sun’s descent, or they would enter the sea, because their land had no mountains. And an army came to them once, and its people said to them, Do not let the sun rise upon you while you are in it. They said, We will not leave until the sun rises. What are these bones? They said, These are the corpses of an army upon whom the sun rose here and they died. He said, So they went fleeing in the land.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement,
h
It will rise upon a people for whom We have not made any shelter against it

, he said: It has reached us that they were in a place where no building could stand, so they would enter into their swarms when the sun rose, until it had set, then they would go out to their livelihoods.

x: Others said: They are the Zanj.
Who said that?

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement,
h
It will look down upon a people for whom We have not made any shield against it
, he said: It is said: They are the Zanj.

x: As for his saying likewise, its meaning is: Then he followed a cause likewise, until he reached the rising of the sun. Likewise: from the connection of followed. Rather, the meaning of the statement is: Then he followed a cause, until he reached the rising of the sun, just as he followed a cause until he reached its setting. And his saying,
h
And We have encompassed what he has with knowledge

, means: And We have encompassed what is at the rising of the sun with knowledge. Nothing of what is there of creation, their conditions, and their causes, or of others, is hidden from us. And with what we said about the meaning of the report, the people of interpretation said.
Who said that?

c: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, his statement report he said:
m: knowledge.

c: Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: the same.

c: Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said:
m: Ibn Zayd said, regarding his statement, Likewise,
h
and We have encompassed what he has with knowledge
, he said: knowledge.

x: God Almighty says: Then he traveled through roads and houses, and took paths.

God Almighty says: Then he traveled through roads and places, and took paths, until he reached between the two barriers. The reciters differed in their reading of this. The majority of the reciters of Medina and some of the Kufians read it as until it reaches bayn al-saddayn with a damma on the seen, and likewise everything in the Qur’an of this type with a damma on the seen.

Some of the reciters of Mecca read it with a fatha on all of it. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala’ used to open the seen in this surah, and closed the seen in Ya-Seen. He used to say: The dam with the fatha is the barrier between you and something, and the dam with the damma is the covering of the eye. As for the Kufians, the majority of their recitation in the entire Qur’an is with a fatha on the seen, except for the statement until it reaches bayn al-saddayn, in which case they closed the seen in particular.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Ikrimah
m: regarding this, what: Ahmad bin Yusuf narrated to us, he said: Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to us, on the authority of Harun, on the authority of Ayoub, on the authority of Ikrimah, he said: Whatever is made by the sons of Adam is the dam, meaning with the fat-ha, and whatever is made by God is the dam. Al-Kisa’i used to say: They are two languages with one meaning. The correct thing to say about that, in my opinion, is that they are two readings that are widespread in the readings of the regions, and two languages that agree on the meaning and do not differ, so whichever of them the reader recites is correct. There is no meaning to the difference that was mentioned by Abu Amr ibn al-Ala and Ikrimah between sadd and sadd, because we did not find any witness to that that clarifies the difference between that according to what was narrated from them.

c: What clarifies that is that all the people of interpretation who narrated to us from them a statement
m: about that, did not narrate to us from any of them a distinction between the fathah and damma of that, and if they differed in meaning, the separation would have been transferred with the interpretation, God willing, but the meaning of that was not separate for them, so the letter is interpreted without a distinction from them between that. As for what was mentioned from Ikrimah about that, the one who narrated that from Ayoub Harun, and there is doubt in his narration, and we do not know that from Ayoub from the narration of his trustworthy companions. The dam and the dam together: the barrier between two things, and here, as mentioned, they are two mountains that blocked what is between them, so Dhul-Qarnayn built a barrier between Yajuj and Majuj and those behind them, to cut off the source of their evil and their chaos from them. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said.

x: Who said that?

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Ata’ Al-Khurasani, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: Until when he reached between the two barriers, he said: The two mountains are the embankment between Gog and Magog, two nations from behind the embankment of Dhul-Qarnayn. He said: The two mountains are Armenia and Azerbaijan.

c: Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: Until he reached between the two mountains. They are two mountains.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Hussein,
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubaid narrated to us, who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say regarding His statement, between the two barriers, meaning between two mountains.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, he said:
m: Between the two dams, he said: They are two mountains. And His saying,
h
And he found

, beyond them, a people who could hardly understand a word. The Almighty says: He found, beyond the two barriers, a people who could hardly understand a word other than their own words. The reciters differed in their reading of the phrase yafqahunu understanding. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra, and some of the people of Kufa, read it as yafqahunu qawlan with a fatha on the qaf and the ya’, from faqahu al-rajul yafqahu fiqhan understanding. The majority of the reciters of Kufa read it as yafqahunu qawlan with a damma on the ya’ and a kasra on the qaf: from afqahu fulan kadha afqahu ifqaha: if you made him understand that. The correct thing to say about this, in my opinion, is that they are two readings that are widespread in the reading of the regions, neither of them contradicting the other. This is because the people about whom the narrator reported this information could have hardly understood what others said about them, so the reading would be correct according to that. It is also possible that, while they were like that, they could hardly understand others for reasons: either by their tongues or by their logic, so the reading according to that would also be correct.

x: And his saying, Indeed, Gog and Magog are
h
corrupters in the land
. The reciters differed in the reading of his saying, Indeed, Gog and Magog are
h
corrupters in the land

. The reciters from the people of Hijaz, Iraq, and others read Indeed, Gog and Magog without a hamza on the basis of fa'ul from yajjat and majjat, and they made the two alifs in them extra, except for Asim bin Abi al-Najud and al-A'raj, for he mentioned that they read it with a hamza in both of them, and they made the hamza in them from the root of the speech, and it is as if they made Yajuj: yaf'ul from ajajat, and ma'juj: maf'ul. The reading that is the correct reading according to us, is Indeed, Gog and Magog with an alif without a hamza, due to the consensus of the proof from the reciters on it, and that it is the well-known speech on the tongues of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of Ru'bah bin al-'Ajaj: If Gog and Magog were together, 'Ad would return and seek help from them, and they are two nations from behind the dam.
And his saying,
h
Corrupters in the land
, the people differed.
Interpretation of the meaning of corruption that God described these two nations with.
Some of them said: They were eating people.
Mention of those who said that:

c: Ahmad ibn al-Waleed al-Ramli told us: Ibrahim ibn Ayoub al-Khawzani told us: al-Waleed ibn Muslim told us:
m: I heard Saeed ibn Abdul Aziz say about His statement, Indeed, Gog and Magog are corrupters on earth, that they used to eat people.

x: Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: Gog and Magog will corrupt on earth, not that they were corrupters on that day.
He mentioned who said that, and he mentioned the description of Dhul-Qarnayn’s following of the reasons mentioned by God in this verse, and he mentioned the reason for his building the dam:

c: Ibn Hamid told us: Salamah told us: Muhammad ibn Ishaq told us:
m: Some of those who narrate the hadiths of the non-Arabs among the People of the Book, who had converted to Islam, told me about what they had inherited from the knowledge of Dhul-Qarnayn, that Dhul-Qarnayn was a man from the people of Egypt whose name was Marzumba ibn Mardaba the Greek, from the descendants of Yunun ibn Japheth ibn Noah.

c: Ibn Humayd told us: Salamah told us: Muhammad ibn Ishaq told us, on the authority of Thawr ibn Yazid, on the authority of Khalid ibn Ma’dan al-Kila’i - and Khalid was a man
m: who had known the people - that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was asked about Dhul-Qarnayn, and he said: A king who wiped the earth from beneath it with means. Khalid said: Umar ibn al-Khattab heard a man say: O Dhul-Qarnayn, so he said: O God, forgive me! Are you not satisfied to be named after the names of the prophets, even if you are named after the names of the angels? If the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said that, then what he said is true, and what contradicts it is false. Ibn Humayd narrated: Salamah narrated: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated:
b.via: Khalid ibn Ma’dan al-Kila’i - and Khalid was a man

c: Someone I do not suspect narrated to me on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih al-Yamani,
m: who had knowledge of the first hadiths, that he used to say: Dhul-Qarnayn was a Roman man, the son of an old woman from among their old women, who had no other children but him, and his name was Alexander. He was called Dhul-Qarnayn because the sides of his head were made of copper. When he reached puberty and was a righteous slave, God, the Almighty, said to him: O Dhul-Qarnayn, I am sending you to the nations of the earth, and they are nations with different languages, and they are all the people of the earth, and among them are two nations between which is the entire length of the earth, and among them are two nations between which is the entire width of the earth, and nations in the middle of the earth, including the jinn and mankind and Gog and Magog. As for the two nations between which is the length of the earth: one is at the setting of the sun, and it is called Nasik. As for the other, it is at its rising, and it is called Mansak. As for the two between which is the width of the earth, there is a nation in the right part of the earth, and it is called Hawil. As for the other one in the left part of the earth, it is a nation called Tawil. When God said that to him, Dhul-Qarnayn said to him: My God, you have summoned me for a great matter that only you can estimate. So tell me about these nations to which you have sent me, with what strength I can overcome them, with what group I can outnumber them, with what trick I can outwit them, with what patience I can endure them, with what tongue I can speak to them, with what hearing I can comprehend their words, with what sight I can penetrate them, with what argument I can argue with them, with what heart I can reason about them, with what wisdom I can manage their affairs, with what equity I can be just between them, with what patience I can be patient with them, with what knowledge I can decide between them, with what science I can perfect their affairs, with what hand I can attack them, with what foot I can trample them, with what strength I can argue with them, with what army I can fight them, and with what kindness I can win them over. For I, my God, do not have anything of what you mentioned that can stand up to them, nor can it overcome them or endure them, and you are the Lord, the Merciful. He does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity, nor Surat al-Kahf 18:94 They said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are
h
corrupters in the land

. So may we assign you an expenditure on condition that you make between us and them a barrier?" burden it beyond its ability, nor does He oppress it nor burden it, but rather You are compassionate towards it and have mercy upon it.
